e-3454.knowledge_point: Finding the Curvature of a Plane Curve Given in Parametric Form
e-3454.problem:
The signed curvature of the plane curve $\mathbf r(t) = \big\langle t, \: \sin t \big\rangle$ is given by

$$
k (t) = \dfrac{\bbox[2pt, border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{AA}}}{\sqrt{ (1+\cos^2 t)^3 } }, \quad t\neq 0.
$$

What is the missing part of the expression?
e-3454.worked_solution:
The signed curvature $k(t)$ of a plane curve $\mathbf r(t) =  \left \langle x(t), y(t) \right \rangle$ is given by

$$
k (t) = \dfrac {x'(t) y''(t) - y'(t) x''(t)} {\big([x'(t)]^2 + [y'(t)]^2\big)^{3/2}}.
$$

Along our curve, we have

$$
x(t) = t, \qquad y(t) = \sin t.
$$

First, we calculate the derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =1,\, & {y}^{′}(t) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ {x}^{″}(t) & =0,\, & {y}^{″}(t) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the signed curvature, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}k(t) & =\frac{1\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)-0\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t}{{({1}^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{-\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{{(1+{cos}^{2}⁡t)}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{-\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{\sqrt{(1+{cos}^{2}⁡t)^{3}}}\end{aligned}
$$

e-3452.knowledge_point: Finding the Radius of Curvature of a Plane Curve Given in Parametric Form
e-3452.problem: Find the radius of curvature for the curve  $\mathbf r(t) =  t \, \mathbf i + \sin t\, \mathbf j$ at $t = \dfrac \pi 2.$
e-3452.worked_solution:
The curvature $\kappa(t)$ of a plane curve $\mathbf r(t) = x(t) \, \mathbf i + y(t)\,\mathbf j$ is given by

$$
\kappa (t) = \dfrac {|x'(t) y''(t) - y'(t) x''(t)|} {\big([x'(t)]^2 + [y'(t)]^2\big)^{3/2}}.
$$

The radius of curvature $R$ is defined as
$R(t) = \dfrac 1 {\kappa(t)}.$

Along our curve, we have

$$
x(t) = t, \qquad y(t) = \sin t.
$$

First, we calculate the derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =1,\, & {y}^{′}(t) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ {x}^{″}(t) & =0,\, & {y}^{″}(t) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the curvature, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{|1\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 0|}{{({1}^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{|\operatorname{sin}⁡t|}{{(1+{cos}^{2}⁡t)}^{3/2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t = \dfrac{\pi}2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\frac{|\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})|}{{(1+{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{(1+{0}^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the radius of curvature at $t = \dfrac{\pi}2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\frac{1}{κ(\frac{\pi }{2})}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

e-3453.knowledge_point: Finding the Curvature of a Plane Curve Given in Cartesian Form
e-3453.problem: Find the curvature of the curve $y = x^3$ at $x=-1.$
e-3453.worked_solution:
The curvature $\kappa(x)$ of a plane curve $y = y(x)$ is given by

$$
\kappa(x) = \dfrac {|y''(x)|} {(1+[y'(x)]^2)^{3/2}}.
$$

First, we calculate $y'(x)$ and $y''(x){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(x) & =3{x}^{2},\, & {y}^{″}(x) & =6x\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the curvature, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(x) & =\frac{|6x|}{{[1+{(3{x}^{2})}^{2}]}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{|6x|}{{(1+9{x}^{4})}^{3/2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $x=-1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(-1) & =\frac{|6(-1)|}{{(1+9(-1)^{4})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{|-6|}{{(1+9)}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{6}{{10}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{6}{10\sqrt{10}} \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{10}}{50}.\end{aligned}
$$

cos⁡t−tsin⁡t

cos⁡t+tsin⁡t

−cos⁡t−tsin⁡t

decision.explanation: Using signed curvature, the numerator is x'y''−y'x''. Here x'=cos(t), x''=−sin(t), y'=−2t, and y''=−2, so the numerator is −2cos(t)−2t sin(t)=2(−cos(t)−t sin(t)). Thus the missing expression is option d.

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\, & {y}^{′}(t) & =-2t \\ {x}^{″}(t) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\, & {y}^{″}(t) & =-2\end{aligned}

$$

Question 1

The signed curvature of the plane curve r(t)=⟨sin⁡t,−t2⟩ is given by k(t)=2⋅(AA)(cos2⁡t+4t2)3. What is the missing part of the expression?

a
cos⁡t−tsin⁡t
b
−tcos⁡t−sin⁡t
c
cos⁡t+tsin⁡t
d
−cos⁡t−tsin⁡t
e
tcos⁡t+sin⁡t
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The signed curvature k(t) of a plane curve r(t)=⟨x(t),y(t)⟩ is given by

k(t)=x′(t)y″(t)−y′(t)x″(t)([x′(t)]2+[y′(t)]2)3/2.

Along our curve, we have

x(t)=sin⁡t,y(t)=−t2.

First, we calculate the derivatives of the components:

x′(t)=cos⁡t,y′(t)=−2tx″(t)=−sin⁡t,y″(t)=−2

Substituting these into the formula for the signed curvature, we get: k(t)=cos⁡t⋅(−2)−(−2t)⋅(−sin⁡t)((cos⁡t)2+(−2t)2)3/2=−2cos⁡t−2tsin⁡t(cos2⁡t+4t2)3/2=2(−cos⁡t−tsin⁡t)(cos2⁡t+4t2)3

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms x'y''−y'x''=cos(t)(−2)−(−2t)(−sin(t))=2(−cos(t)−t sin(t)). Therefore the missing expression is option d. The observed incorrect submission selected b, not d.

content.problem:
The signed curvature of the plane curve $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-{t}^{2}⟩$ is given by

$$
k(t)=\frac{2\cdot (\,\,)}{\sqrt{({cos}^{2}⁡t+4{t}^{2})^{3}}}.
$$

What is the missing part of the expression?
content.worked_solution:
The signed curvature $k(t)$ of a plane curve $r(t)=⟨x(t),y(t)⟩$ is given by

$$
k(t)=\frac{{x}^{′}(t){y}^{″}(t)-{y}^{′}(t){x}^{″}(t)}{([{x}^{′}(t)]^{2}+[{y}^{′}(t)]^{2})^{3/2}}.
$$

Along our curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,y(t)=-{t}^{2}.
$$

First, we calculate the derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\, & {y}^{′}(t) & =-2t \\ {x}^{″}(t) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\, & {y}^{″}(t) & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the signed curvature, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}k(t) & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (-2)-(-2t)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}{{((\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(-2t)^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2t\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{{({cos}^{2}⁡t+4{t}^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{2(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}{\sqrt{({cos}^{2}⁡t+4{t}^{2})^{3}}}\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem:
The curvature of the plane curve $r(t)=-t\,i+({t}^{2}+1)\,j$ is given by 

$$
κ(t)=\frac{2}{}.
$$

 
What is the missing part of the expression?
after.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ(t)$ of a plane curve $r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{|{x}^{′}(t){y}^{″}(t)-{y}^{′}(t){x}^{″}(t)|}{([{x}^{′}(t)]^{2}+[{y}^{′}(t)]^{2})^{3/2}}.
$$

Along our curve, we have

$$
x(t)=-t,\,y(t)={t}^{2}+1.
$$

First, we calculate the derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =-1,\, & {y}^{′}(t) & =2t \\ {x}^{″}(t) & =0,\, & {y}^{″}(t) & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the curvature, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{|(-1)\cdot 2-2t\cdot 0|}{{((-1)^{2}+(2t)^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{|-2|}{{(1+4{t}^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{{(1+4{t}^{2})}^{3}}}\end{aligned}

content.problem:
The curvature of the plane curve $r(t)=-t\,i+({t}^{2}+1)\,j$ is given by 

$$
κ(t)=\frac{2}{}.
$$

 
What is the missing part of the expression?
content.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ(t)$ of a plane curve $r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{|{x}^{′}(t){y}^{″}(t)-{y}^{′}(t){x}^{″}(t)|}{([{x}^{′}(t)]^{2}+[{y}^{′}(t)]^{2})^{3/2}}.
$$

Along our curve, we have

$$
x(t)=-t,\,y(t)={t}^{2}+1.
$$

First, we calculate the derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =-1,\, & {y}^{′}(t) & =2t \\ {x}^{″}(t) & =0,\, & {y}^{″}(t) & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the curvature, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{|(-1)\cdot 2-2t\cdot 0|}{{((-1)^{2}+(2t)^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{|-2|}{{(1+4{t}^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{{(1+4{t}^{2})}^{3}}}\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
The curvature of the plane curve $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+t\,j$ is given by 

$$
κ(t)=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{},\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

 
What is the missing part of the expression?
after.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ(t)$ of a plane curve $r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{|{x}^{′}(t){y}^{″}(t)-{y}^{′}(t){x}^{″}(t)|}{([{x}^{′}(t)]^{2}+[{y}^{′}(t)]^{2})^{3/2}}.
$$

Along our curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(t)=t.
$$

First, we calculate the derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\, & {y}^{′}(t) & =1 \\ {x}^{″}(t) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\, & {y}^{″}(t) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the curvature, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{|(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot 0-(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot 1|}{{((\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+{1}^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{|\operatorname{cos}⁡t|}{{({sin}^{2}⁡t+1)}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{\sqrt{{({sin}^{2}⁡t+1)}^{3}}}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we removed the absolute value because cosine is positive for $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].$

Question 4

The signed curvature of the plane curve r(t)=⟨−ln⁡t,t⟩ is given by k(t)=AA(1+t2)3,t>0. What is the missing part of the expression?

a
t
b
−t
c
t3+t2
d
t2
e
t3−t2
Submit

decision.explanation: Here x'=−1/t, x''=1/t², y'=1, and y''=0. The signed curvature is (−1/t²)/(1/t²+1)^(3/2). Since t>0, this simplifies to −t/(1+t²)^(3/2), so the missing numerator is −t.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
The signed curvature of the plane curve $r(t)=⟨-\operatorname{ln}⁡t,\,t⟩$ is given by

$$
k(t)=\frac{}{\sqrt{(1+{t}^{2})^{3}}},\,t>0.
$$

What is the missing part of the expression?
after.worked_solution:
The signed curvature $k(t)$ of a plane curve $r(t)=⟨x(t),y(t)⟩$ is given by

$$
k(t)=\frac{{x}^{′}(t){y}^{″}(t)-{y}^{′}(t){x}^{″}(t)}{([{x}^{′}(t)]^{2}+[{y}^{′}(t)]^{2})^{3/2}}.
$$

Along our curve, we have

$$
x(t)=-\operatorname{ln}⁡t,\,y(t)=t.
$$

First, we calculate the derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =-{t}^{-1},\, & {y}^{′}(t) & =1 \\ {x}^{″}(t) & ={t}^{-2},\, & {y}^{″}(t) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the signed curvature, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}k(t) & =\frac{-{t}^{-1}\cdot 0-1\cdot ({t}^{-2})}{{((-{t}^{-1})^{2}+(1)^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{-{t}^{-2}}{{({t}^{-2}+1)}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{-{t}^{-2}\cdot ({t}^{2})^{3/2}}{{(1+{t}^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{-{t}^{-2}\cdot |t{|}^{3}}{{(1+{t}^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{-{t}^{-2}\cdot {t}^{3}}{{(1+{t}^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{-t}{\sqrt{(1+{t}^{2})^{3}}}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we removed the absolute value because $t>0.$

$R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}.$

$$

$$

$$

after.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ(t)$ of a plane curve $r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{|{x}^{′}(t){y}^{″}(t)-{y}^{′}(t){x}^{″}(t)|}{([{x}^{′}(t)]^{2}+[{y}^{′}(t)]^{2})^{3/2}}.
$$

The radius of curvature $R$ is defined as
$R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}.$

Along our curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\,y(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t).
$$

First, we calculate the derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),\, & {y}^{′}(t) & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ {x}^{″}(t) & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\, & {y}^{″}(t) & =-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the curvature, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{|2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\cdot (-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))-(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))|}{{((2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))^{2}+(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{|-8{cos}^{2}⁡(2t)-8{sin}^{2}⁡(2t)|}{{(4{cos}^{2}⁡(2t)+4{sin}^{2}⁡(2t))}^{3/2}} \\  & =1\end{aligned}

$$

The curvature $κ(x)$ of a plane curve $y=y(x)$ is given by

$$
κ(x)=\frac{|{y}^{″}(x)|}{(1+[{y}^{′}(x)]^{2})^{3/2}}.

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x+x\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\, & {y}^{″}(x) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡x-x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(x) & =\frac{|2\operatorname{cos}⁡x-x\operatorname{sin}⁡x|}{{[1+{(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+x\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}^{2}]}^{3/2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $x=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(0) & =\frac{|2\operatorname{cos}⁡0-0|}{{(1+0)}^{3/2}} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$
